scenes.narration: Should a robot keep one model of the world, or several?
We propose a federation of world models: members that each predict a bounded part of the world, couplers that relate them, contracts that check every message, and one shared planner.
On a robot reaching for a glass, the arm is an analytical member, the gripper a learned one; a coupler at the wrist selects the regime, and the glass pose travels as a hypothesis under contract.
In highway driving, the federation succeeded on sixty-two percent of withheld episodes, the monolith on fifty-seven.
In transport, ninety-nine percent on a pairing never seen, against forty for the monolith.
In tool use, no difference at all: a boundary that buys nothing is a result too.
Boundaries pay when the robot acts where it has no data, and when a part must change without breaking the rest. Whether composition earns its cost is now a testable question, and we give the test.
